decks.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Part 1: Tissues and tissue systems
goals: Describe simple and complex permanent tissues
Describe the epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems

slides.heading: Anatomy of flowering plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — tissues: how cells of one kind work together.

visual.alt: Flow from tissue to meristematic and permanent tissues

slides.narration: Anatomy is the study of internal structure. A tissue is a group of similar cells, usually with a common origin, that perform a common function. Plant tissues are of two broad kinds: those that divide, called meristematic, and those that have stopped dividing, called permanent.

slides.heading: Meristematic tissues
slides.body_md: Cells of a **meristem** divide continually. **Apical meristems** at the root and shoot tips cause **primary growth** in length. **Intercalary meristems** at the base of leaves and internodes, as in grasses, allow regrowth.

rows: Base of leaves or internodes, as in grasses

visual.alt: Table of apical and intercalary meristems

slides.narration: Meristematic cells are small, thin walled and full of dense cytoplasm, with prominent nuclei. Apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots make the plant longer. Intercalary meristems, found in grasses, explain why a mown lawn grows back from the base of its leaves.

slides.heading: Simple permanent tissues
slides.body_md: Simple tissues have **one kind of cell**: **parenchyma** (living, thin walls), **collenchyma** (living, corners thickened) and **sclerenchyma** (dead, lignified walls).

slides.narration: Parenchyma is the most common tissue. Its thin walled living cells carry out photosynthesis, storage and secretion. Collenchyma cells are thickened at the corners and support young stems and leaf stalks. Sclerenchyma cells are dead, with thick lignified walls, and give strength. Fibres and sclereids are its two kinds.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: real size from a micrograph
slides.body_md: A parenchyma cell measures 21 mm across on a print at 600 times magnification, and a sclereid measures 45 mm at 900 times. Find their real widths.
bullets: Real size = image size $\div$ magnification: $\dfrac{21 \times 1000}{600} = 35$ micrometres.
Sclereid: $\dfrac{45 \times 1000}{900} = 50$ micrometres.
Both are tens of micrometres, the usual size of plant cells.

visual.alt: Worked table: 35 and 50 micrometres

slides.narration: To find the real size, divide the size in the picture by the magnification and convert millimetres to micrometres. The parenchyma cell works out to thirty five micrometres, and the sclereid to fifty micrometres.

slides.heading: Complex tissue: xylem
slides.body_md: **Xylem** conducts **water and minerals** and gives support. Elements: **tracheids**, **vessels**, **xylem fibres** (all dead) and **xylem parenchyma** (living). The first-formed xylem is **protoxylem**, the later is **metaxylem**.

rows: Long tubes of cells with perforated ends

visual.alt: Table of the four elements of xylem

slides.narration: Xylem has more than one kind of cell, so it is a complex tissue. Tracheids and vessels carry water and are dead, with lignified walls. Xylem fibres give support, and xylem parenchyma is the only living part. In stems the protoxylem lies towards the pith, which is called endarch, while in roots it lies towards the outside, which is exarch.

slides.heading: Complex tissue: phloem
slides.body_md: **Phloem** conducts **food** from leaves to other parts. Elements: **sieve tube elements**, **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**.

rows: Long tubes with sieve plates; peripheral cytoplasm and no nucleus
Nucleated; keep the sieve tube functioning
Stores food; absent in most monocots

visual.alt: Table of the four elements of phloem

slides.narration: Sieve tube elements are long tubes with perforated end walls called sieve plates. At maturity they lack a nucleus, but each is helped by a companion cell with a nucleus. Phloem parenchyma stores food and is absent in most monocots. Phloem fibres, also called bast fibres, are dead and give strength.

slides.heading: The epidermal tissue system
slides.body_md: The **epidermis** is the outermost layer, covered by a **cuticle** in aerial parts. It bears **stomata**, **root hairs** and **trichomes**. Each stoma has two **guard cells**: **bean-shaped** in dicots, **dumbbell-shaped** in grasses.

visual.alt: Table comparing guard cells and stomata of dicot and grass leaves

slides.narration: The epidermis protects the plant and limits water loss. Stomata control gas exchange and transpiration, and each pore is guarded by two guard cells. Guard cells are bean shaped in dicots and dumbbell shaped in grasses. Root hairs are outgrowths of root epidermal cells that absorb water, and trichomes are hairs on the stem that reduce water loss.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: stomatal density
slides.body_md: In a field of view of 0.25 square millimetres, a student counts 5 stomata on the upper epidermis of a dicot leaf and 20 on the lower. Find the density on each surface and the ratio.
bullets: Upper: $\dfrac{5}{0.25} = 20$ per square millimetre.
Lower: $\dfrac{20}{0.25} = 80$ per square millimetre.
Ratio lower to upper: $\dfrac{80}{20} = 4$.

visual.alt: Worked table: densities 20 and 80 per square millimetre

slides.narration: Divide each count by the area of the field. Five stomata in a quarter of a square millimetre is twenty per square millimetre above, and twenty stomata is eighty below. The lower surface has four times as many, as expected in a dicot leaf.

slides.heading: The ground tissue system
slides.body_md: All tissues except the epidermis and the vascular bundles form the **ground tissue**: **cortex**, **pericycle**, **pith** and **medullary rays** in stems and roots; **mesophyll** in leaves.

rows: Epidermis, cuticle, stomata, root hairs, trichomes
Cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays; mesophyll in leaves
Xylem and phloem (and cambium in dicot stems)

visual.alt: Table of the three tissue systems

slides.narration: Ground tissue is mostly parenchyma, though it may be collenchyma or sclerenchyma. In stems and roots it includes the cortex, the pericycle, the pith and the medullary rays. In leaves it is the mesophyll, which is rich in chloroplasts and carries out photosynthesis.

slides.heading: The vascular tissue system
slides.body_md: Xylem and phloem form **vascular bundles**. In roots they are **radial**. In stems and leaves they are **conjoint**, on the same radius: **open** when **cambium** lies between them (dicot stems), **closed** when it is absent (monocot stems).

visual.alt: Radial, conjoint open and conjoint closed vascular bundles

slides.narration: In a radial bundle, as in roots, xylem and phloem lie on different radii and alternate. In a conjoint bundle they lie together on the same radius, with phloem outside. If a strip of cambium separates them, the bundle is open, as in dicot stems. If there is no cambium, the bundle is closed, as in monocot stems.

slides.heading: Quick check: vascular bundles
slides.body_md: Classify the bundle.
slides.narration: Quick check. Is there cambium between the xylem and phloem?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Meristems divide: apical (tips, primary growth) and intercalary (grass leaf base).
Simple tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma (fibres and sclereids).
Complex tissues: xylem (tracheids, vessels, fibres, parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres).
Epidermal system: cuticle, stomata with guard cells, root hairs, trichomes.
Ground system: cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays, mesophyll.
Vascular bundles: radial, conjoint open, conjoint closed.

rows: Epidermis, cuticle, stomata, root hairs, trichomes
Cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays; mesophyll in leaves
Xylem and phloem (and cambium in dicot stems)

visual.alt: Table of the three tissue systems

slides.narration: To recap: meristems divide, and permanent tissues are simple or complex. Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma are simple. Xylem and phloem are complex. The three tissue systems are the epidermal, the ground and the vascular, and bundles are radial, conjoint open or conjoint closed.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **living or dead** for every tissue and element.
Remember **xylem carries water** and **phloem carries food**.
Link **open bundles** to cambium in **dicot stems**.
Give the **shape of guard cells** with the plant group.
slides.narration: Exam tips. State whether each tissue is living or dead. Remember that xylem carries water and phloem carries food. Link open bundles with cambium in dicot stems. And give the shape of guard cells with the plant group.

decks.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Part 2: Dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf
goals: Describe the transverse section of a dicot and a monocot root
Compare the anatomy of dicot and monocot stems
Describe the anatomy of dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves

slides.heading: Looking inside organs
slides.body_md: Part 2 — transverse sections of root, stem and leaf.

visual.alt: Flow from root to stem to leaf, naming the main anatomical feature of each

slides.narration: We now use the tissues from part one to read transverse sections of the main organs. Each organ has an epidermis, a ground tissue and vascular tissue, arranged in a pattern that depends on the organ and on whether the plant is a dicot or a monocot.

slides.heading: Dicot root
slides.body_md: Epidermis with **root hairs**, a wide **cortex**, an **endodermis** with **Casparian strips**, a **pericycle**, **two to four** patches of **exarch xylem** alternating with phloem, and a **small pith**.

slides.narration: The endodermis is a single layer of barrel shaped cells whose walls carry waxy bands of suberin, the Casparian strips. Inside it, the pericycle gives rise to lateral roots. Xylem and phloem lie on different radii, with conjunctive tissue between them. The pith is small or absent.

slides.heading: Monocot root
slides.body_md: The same plan as the dicot root, but with **more than six** xylem bundles (**polyarch**) and a **large, well developed pith**.

visual.alt: Labelled transverse section of a monocot root with eight xylem patches and a large pith

slides.narration: The monocot root looks much like the dicot root. The differences are the number of xylem bundles, which is more than six, and the pith, which is large and well developed.

slides.heading: Quick check: roots
slides.body_md: Decide dicot or monocot from the section.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the xylem patches and look at the pith.

slides.heading: Root: dicot and monocot compared
slides.body_md: Both roots have **radial** bundles and **exarch** xylem; they differ in the number of xylem arms and in the pith.

rows: Epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial bundles, exarch xylem

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot roots

slides.narration: Root xylem is exarch, meaning the protoxylem lies towards the outside. Dicot roots have two to four xylem patches, which are called diarch to tetrarch, and a small pith. Monocot roots have more than six, called polyarch, and a large pith.

slides.heading: Dicot stem
slides.body_md: **Epidermis** with cuticle and trichomes, **collenchymatous hypodermis**, **cortex**, **endodermis** (starch sheath), **pericycle**, **medullary rays**, a **ring** of **conjoint, open, endarch** bundles, and a **large pith**.

visual.alt: Labelled transverse section of a dicot stem with a ring of conjoint open vascular bundles

slides.narration: The dicot stem has a few layers of collenchyma just beneath the epidermis. The innermost cortical layer, rich in starch, is the endodermis. Vascular bundles lie in a ring, each with phloem outside, cambium in the middle and xylem inside, with the protoxylem towards the pith. Parenchyma between bundles forms the medullary rays.

slides.heading: Monocot stem
slides.body_md: **Sclerenchymatous hypodermis**; a large, undifferentiated **ground tissue**; **many scattered** bundles, **conjoint and closed**, each with a **sclerenchymatous sheath**; **no phloem parenchyma**; a **water-containing cavity** in each bundle.

visual.alt: Labelled transverse section of a monocot stem with scattered conjoint closed vascular bundles and one enlarged bundle

slides.narration: In the monocot stem the bundles are scattered through the ground tissue rather than in a ring, and they are smaller and more crowded near the edge. Each is surrounded by a sheath of sclerenchyma. There is no cambium, so the bundles are closed, and phloem parenchyma is absent. A water filled cavity lies inside each bundle.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting bundles
slides.body_md: A student counts 30 vascular bundles in a field of 5 square millimetres of a maize stem section. Estimate the bundles in a whole section of 12 square millimetres.
bullets: Density: $\dfrac{30}{5} = 6$ bundles per square millimetre.
Whole section: $6 \times 12 = 72$ bundles.
This assumes the bundles are spread evenly; they are in fact more crowded near the edge, so it is only an estimate.

visual.alt: Worked table: 72 bundles estimated

slides.narration: First find the number of bundles per square millimetre by dividing the count by the area. Thirty bundles in five square millimetres is six per square millimetre. Multiplying by twelve square millimetres gives seventy two. Since bundles crowd towards the edge, this is only an estimate.

slides.heading: Stem: dicot and monocot compared
slides.body_md: Ring of **open** bundles with **collenchymatous** hypodermis in dicots; **scattered closed** bundles with **sclerenchymatous** hypodermis in monocots.

rows: Cortex, endodermis, pericycle, medullary rays, pith
Few, in a ring; conjoint, open
Many, scattered; conjoint, closed, with sheath

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot stems

slides.narration: Dicot stems have a ring of few bundles, a collenchymatous hypodermis and differentiated ground tissue. Monocot stems have many scattered bundles, a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and ground tissue that is not differentiated. Dicot bundles are open, and monocot bundles are closed.

slides.heading: Dicot leaf
slides.body_md: **Upper and lower epidermis** with cuticle and **stomata** (more below). **Mesophyll**: **palisade** (upper, elongated, chloroplast-rich) and **spongy** parenchyma (lower, air spaces). **Vascular bundles** in veins, each with a **bundle sheath**.

visual.alt: Labelled transverse section of a dicot leaf with palisade and spongy parenchyma, vein and stoma

slides.narration: The dicot leaf is dorsiventral, meaning its two sides differ. The palisade cells, close to the upper surface, are tall and tightly packed and carry most of the chloroplasts. The spongy cells below are loosely arranged with air spaces connected to the stomata. In the vein, xylem faces the upper side and phloem the lower.

slides.heading: Leaf: dorsiventral and isobilateral
slides.body_md: In an **isobilateral** (grass) leaf, stomata are on **both** surfaces and the mesophyll is **not differentiated**. **Bulliform cells** on the upper epidermis help the leaf **roll** in dry weather.

rows: Bulliform cells on the upper epidermis

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot leaves

slides.narration: Monocot leaves are usually isobilateral. Stomata are about equally common on both surfaces, and the mesophyll cells are alike. Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells in the upper epidermis. When they lose water the leaf curls inward, which cuts down water loss.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: layers of a leaf
slides.body_md: In a leaf section the upper epidermis is 20 micrometres thick, the palisade 70, the spongy layer 90 and the lower epidermis 20. Find the leaf thickness and the share taken by mesophyll.
bullets: Thickness: $20 + 70 + 90 + 20 = 200$ micrometres.
Mesophyll: $70 + 90 = 160$ micrometres.
Share: $\dfrac{160}{200} \times 100 = 80$ percent; the palisade alone is 35 percent.

visual.alt: Worked table: total 200 micrometres, mesophyll 80 percent

slides.narration: Add the four layers to get the thickness, two hundred micrometres. The mesophyll is the palisade plus the spongy layer, one hundred and sixty micrometres, which is four fifths of the leaf. This is where photosynthesis takes place.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a leaf
slides.body_md: Name the lettered layer in the leaf section.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which lettered tissue is made of tall, closely packed cells below the upper surface?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Dicot root: 2 to 4 xylem patches, small pith; monocot root: more than 6, large pith; both have endodermis with Casparian strips, exarch xylem.
Dicot stem: collenchymatous hypodermis, ring of conjoint open endarch bundles, large pith, medullary rays.
Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, many scattered conjoint closed bundles with sheaths, no phloem parenchyma.
Dicot leaf: palisade and spongy mesophyll, more stomata below, dorsiventral.
Monocot leaf: isobilateral, stomata on both surfaces, bulliform cells.

rows: Cortex, endodermis, pericycle, medullary rays, pith
Few, in a ring; conjoint, open
Many, scattered; conjoint, closed, with sheath

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot stems

slides.narration: To recap: roots have radial bundles and exarch xylem, with polyarch xylem and a large pith in monocots. Dicot stems have a ring of open bundles, and monocot stems have scattered closed bundles. The dicot leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll, while the monocot leaf is isobilateral with bulliform cells.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Label **from outside to inside** in the same order as the section.
Mention **Casparian strips** in the endodermis of roots.
Write **closed** or **open** for bundles and give the reason (cambium).
For leaves give **palisade towards the upper surface**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Label parts from the outside inward, in the order seen in the section. Mention Casparian strips in the root endodermis. Say whether bundles are open or closed and give the reason, which is cambium. And place the palisade tissue towards the upper surface of the leaf.

notes.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Plant tissues and tissue systems
sections.body_md:
Anatomy is the study of internal structure. A **tissue** is a group of similar cells, usually of common origin, that perform a common function. This chapter deals with the **primary** structure of the plant body; secondary growth is not part of this syllabus.

**Meristematic tissues.** Cells divide continually; they are small, thin-walled and rich in cytoplasm. **Apical meristems** at the tips of roots and shoots give **primary growth** in length. **Intercalary meristems**, at the base of leaves or internodes (grasses), allow regrowth after grazing or mowing.

**Permanent tissues** have stopped dividing and are **simple** (one kind of cell) or **complex** (more than one kind).
- **Parenchyma:** living, thin-walled cellulose cells, roundish, with small intercellular spaces; photosynthesis (chlorenchyma), storage and secretion.
- **Collenchyma:** living, with **thickened corners** (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin); may contain chloroplasts; supports young stems and petioles; found beneath the epidermis of dicot stems.
- **Sclerenchyma:** dead cells with thick **lignified** walls and a narrow lumen; **fibres** (long, pointed) and **sclereids** (spherical, oval or cylindrical; seen in fruit walls of nuts, pulp of guava, pear and sapota, seed coats of legumes and in tea leaves); give mechanical strength.
- **Xylem** (complex) conducts **water and minerals** and supports: **tracheids**, **vessels**, **xylem fibres** (dead, lignified) and **xylem parenchyma** (living). The first-formed xylem is **protoxylem** and the later is **metaxylem**. In stems the protoxylem lies towards the pith (**endarch**); in roots it lies towards the periphery (**exarch**).
- **Phloem** (complex) conducts **food**: **sieve tube elements** (long tubes with perforated end walls, the sieve plates; peripheral cytoplasm and no nucleus at maturity), **companion cells** (nucleated; keep the sieve tube functioning), **phloem parenchyma** (absent in most monocots) and **phloem fibres** (bast fibres; dead, lignified).

**Tissue systems.** (1) **Epidermal system:** the epidermis (a single layer, covered by a waxy **cuticle** in aerial parts), **stomata** (a pore bounded by two **guard cells**, bean-shaped in dicots and dumbbell-shaped in grasses, sometimes with subsidiary cells), **root hairs** (unicellular outgrowths that absorb water and minerals) and **trichomes** (multicellular hairs on stems that reduce water loss). (2) **Ground tissue system:** all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles: cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in stems and roots; mesophyll in leaves. (3) **Vascular system:** xylem and phloem (and, in dicot stems, cambium). **Radial** bundles (roots) have xylem and phloem on different radii; **conjoint** bundles (stems and leaves) have them on the same radius, **open** if cambium lies between them (dicot stems) and **closed** if not (monocot stems).

key_terms.definition_md: Tissue whose cells divide continually: apical at root and shoot tips, intercalary at the base of leaves or internodes.
A dead, thick-walled sclerenchyma cell of rounded shape, as in the pulp of pear and guava.
A vascular bundle with xylem and phloem on the same radius, as in stems and leaves.
A conjoint bundle with cambium between xylem and phloem, as in dicot stems.
Xylem with the protoxylem towards the pith, as in stems.

sections.heading: 2. Anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf
sections.body_md:
**Dicot root** (e.g. sunflower), transverse section from outside: the **epidermis** with unicellular **root hairs**; the **cortex**, several layers of thin-walled parenchyma; the **endodermis**, a single layer of barrel-shaped cells with **Casparian strips** of suberin on their walls; the **pericycle**, a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma from which lateral roots arise; a **small pith**; and **conjunctive tissue** between the xylem and phloem. There are usually **two to four** patches of **exarch xylem** (diarch to tetrarch) alternating with phloem patches (radial bundles). **Monocot root:** the same plan, but **more than six** xylem bundles (**polyarch**) and a **large, well-developed pith**.

**Dicot stem** (sunflower): epidermis with cuticle and trichomes, a few stomata; **hypodermis** of collenchyma; **cortex** of parenchyma with a few layers; **endodermis** (starch sheath) as the innermost cortical layer; **pericycle** as semilunar patches of sclerenchyma over the bundles; **medullary rays** between the bundles; **vascular bundles in a ring**, **conjoint, open and endarch**; a large **pith** of rounded parenchyma. **Monocot stem** (maize): **sclerenchymatous hypodermis**; a large, **undifferentiated ground tissue** of parenchyma; **many scattered** vascular bundles, each surrounded by a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath**; bundles **conjoint and closed**, often with a **water-containing cavity**; **phloem parenchyma absent**; smaller and more numerous bundles near the periphery.

**Dicot leaf** (**dorsiventral**): **upper and lower epidermis** with cuticle, with **more stomata on the lower** surface; **mesophyll** differentiated into **palisade parenchyma** (adaxial, elongated cells arranged vertically, chloroplast-rich) and **spongy parenchyma** (abaxial, oval or round, loosely arranged, with large air spaces and connecting to the stomata); **vascular bundles** in the veins and midrib, each surrounded by a thick-walled **bundle sheath**; **xylem towards the upper** and **phloem towards the lower** side. The **monocot leaf** is **isobilateral**: stomata are present on **both** surfaces in about equal numbers, the mesophyll is **not differentiated**, vascular bundles are nearly the same size (parallel venation), and the upper epidermis has **bulliform cells** (large, empty, colourless) that help the leaf roll inwards to minimise water loss.

key_terms.definition_md: A band of suberin on the radial and transverse walls of endodermal cells of the root.
Layer inside the endodermis of the root; lateral roots arise from it.
A leaf whose upper and lower sides differ; mesophyll is palisade above and spongy below.
A leaf (usually monocot) with stomata on both surfaces and undifferentiated mesophyll.
A large, empty, colourless cell of the upper epidermis in grass leaves that helps the leaf roll in dry weather.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying collenchyma is dead or lignified (it is living, with corners thickened by cellulose and pectin).
- Writing that phloem fibres or companion cells conduct food (the sieve tube elements conduct; the others help or support).
- Placing xylem outside the phloem in a conjoint bundle (phloem is outside, towards the periphery, in a stem).
- Calling the dicot stem bundle closed (it has cambium, so it is open).
- Giving a small pith for a monocot root (it is large, and the xylem is polyarch).
- Putting palisade tissue towards the lower surface of a dicot leaf.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a tissue and its living or dead nature, shape of guard cells, type of vascular bundle.
- 2–3-mark answers: apical and intercalary meristems; xylem and phloem elements; differences between dicot and monocot roots or stems.
- 5-mark answers: the three simple tissues; tissue systems; a labelled section of a dicot stem, a monocot stem or a dicot leaf.
- Numericals: real size from magnification, stomatal density, bundle counts, layer thickness — show each step.

questions.solution_md: Collenchyma is a living tissue with corners thickened by cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; it may contain chloroplasts and supports young petioles — option (b).

options.text_md: collenchyma, living cells with thickened corners
phloem fibres, long and still alive

Its cells are living and have thin cellulose walls with large vacuoles.

questions.stem_md: A tube made of many cells joined end to end, dead at maturity and with perforated end walls, carries water in a flowering plant. This element is a

questions.solution_md: Each sieve tube element is associated with a nucleated companion cell that keeps it functioning — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a transverse section of a root, the first-formed xylem elements lie towards the periphery; in a stem section they lie towards the pith. These two arrangements are called respectively
questions.solution_md: Root xylem is exarch (protoxylem outside); stem xylem is endarch (protoxylem towards the pith) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student removes a narrow ring of outer tissue, including the phloem but leaving the xylem, from a young herbaceous stem. A few weeks later the region just above the ring is swollen with sugars, while the stem keeps taking up water. This shows that

options.text_md: phloem carries food from the leaves, whereas xylem continues to carry water
xylem carries food from the leaves, whereas phloem carries water
the cortex alone carries both food and water to the roots
companion cells carry water up the stem without any xylem

questions.solution_md: Phloem conducts food from the leaves; when it is cut, food piles up above the cut. Water still rises through the intact xylem — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A peel from a maize leaf shows each stoma with two dumbbell-shaped guard cells. A peel from a sunflower leaf will show

options.text_md: a sclerenchyma ring around each pore
no guard cells, because dicots lack stomata

questions.solution_md: Guard cells are dumbbell-shaped in grasses and bean-shaped in dicots such as sunflower — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these belongs to the ground tissue system of a stem?
questions.solution_md: The ground tissue system includes cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays; stomata and cuticle are epidermal and xylem is vascular — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Xylem and phloem on the same radius make a conjoint bundle; cambium between them makes it open — option (c).

On the same radius, with cambium between them
In scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths
On different radii, alternating with each other

questions.solution_md: False. Collenchyma is living, with corners thickened by cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.

questions.solution_md: True. They are dead, lignified water-conducting cells.

questions.solution_md: Closed.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between apical and intercalary meristems on the basis of their position and the growth they bring about.

answer.model_answer_md: **Apical meristems** lie at the **tips of roots and shoots** and make the plant longer; this is **primary growth**. **Intercalary meristems** lie at the **base of leaves or internodes**, as in **grasses**, and allow the leaf or internode to grow again after it has been cut or grazed.

questions.solution_md: Position and effect.

Intercalary: base of leaves or internodes; regrowth

questions.stem_md: A strip taken from a young leaf stalk and a piece of a coconut shell are examined. Name the tissue that makes up each and give one difference between them.

answer.model_answer_md: The **young leaf stalk** has **collenchyma**, made of **living** cells whose **corners are thickened** with cellulose and pectin, giving flexible support. The **coconut shell** has **sclerenchyma**, made of **dead** cells with **thick lignified walls** and a narrow cavity, giving rigid strength.

questions.solution_md: Collenchyma versus sclerenchyma.

marking_scheme.step: A difference: living versus dead, or the wall thickening

questions.stem_md: Name the four elements of xylem and state which one is living.

answer.model_answer_md: The four elements of **xylem** are **tracheids**, **vessels**, **xylem fibres** and **xylem parenchyma**. Tracheids, vessels and fibres are **dead** and have lignified walls. **Xylem parenchyma** is the only **living** element; it stores food and helps in radial conduction of water.

questions.solution_md: Four elements; parenchyma living.

questions.stem_md: Name the four elements of phloem and say what is special about a mature sieve tube element.

answer.model_answer_md: The elements of **phloem** are **sieve tube elements**, **companion cells**, **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres**. A mature **sieve tube element** is a long tube with perforated end walls, the **sieve plates**; it has peripheral cytoplasm and **no nucleus**, and depends on its companion cell.

questions.solution_md: Four elements; sieve tube features.

questions.stem_md: Describe the epidermal tissue system, naming three structures found in it and one role of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **epidermis** is the outermost layer, covered by a **cuticle** in aerial parts, which reduces water loss. It bears **stomata**, pores with two guard cells that control gas exchange and transpiration, and **root hairs**, which absorb water and minerals. **Trichomes** on the stem are hairs that cut down loss of water.

questions.solution_md: Epidermis, cuticle, stomata, root hairs, trichomes.

marking_scheme.step: Stomata, root hairs or trichomes with roles

questions.stem_md: Name the three simple permanent tissues and state the structure and function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Parenchyma** has living, thin-walled, roundish cells and carries out photosynthesis, storage and secretion. **Collenchyma** has living cells with **corners thickened** by cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, and supports young stems and petioles. **Sclerenchyma** has **dead** cells with thick lignified walls and a narrow cavity, as fibres or sclereids, and gives mechanical strength.

questions.solution_md: Three tissues, structure and function.

questions.stem_md: Compare xylem and phloem on any three points.

answer.model_answer_md: **Xylem** conducts **water and minerals** upward and gives support; **phloem** conducts **food** from the leaves to other parts. Xylem has tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma, mostly **dead**; phloem has sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres, with **living** conducting cells. In a stem the protoxylem is towards the pith, and the phloem lies outside the xylem.

questions.solution_md: Function, elements, living or dead.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish radial, conjoint open and conjoint closed vascular bundles, with the organ in which each is found.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **radial** bundle, found in **roots**, xylem and phloem lie on **different radii**, alternating. In a **conjoint open** bundle, found in **dicot stems**, xylem and phloem lie on the **same radius** with a strip of **cambium** between them. In a **conjoint closed** bundle, found in **monocot stems**, they lie on the same radius but there is **no cambium**.

questions.solution_md: Three types of bundle with organs.

marking_scheme.step: Conjoint open with cambium, dicot stem
Conjoint closed without cambium, monocot stem

questions.stem_md: What is the ground tissue system? Name its parts in the stem and in the leaf.

answer.model_answer_md: The **ground tissue system** includes all tissues except the **epidermis** and the **vascular bundles**. It is mostly parenchyma, though it may also be collenchyma or sclerenchyma. In stems and roots it includes the **cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays**. In leaves it is the **mesophyll**, rich in chloroplasts, which carries out photosynthesis.

questions.solution_md: Definition; stem parts; mesophyll.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: all except epidermis and bundles

questions.stem_md: Describe the three simple permanent tissues of plants with their structure, location and function, and explain why sclerenchyma is called a dead tissue.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Parenchyma** has thin-walled, living, roundish or polygonal cells with small intercellular spaces. It forms the cortex, pith and mesophyll, and carries out photosynthesis, storage and secretion.

**Collenchyma** has living cells with corners thickened by cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; some have chloroplasts. It lies below the epidermis of dicot stems and in petioles, and gives flexible support to young parts.

**Sclerenchyma** has cells with thick, lignified walls and a narrow cavity, as long pointed **fibres** or rounded **sclereids** (fruit walls of nuts, pulp of pear and guava, seed coats). It gives strength. It is called dead because the lignified walls prevent exchange, so the **protoplast is lost** at maturity.

questions.solution_md: Three tissues with structure, location, function; why sclerenchyma is dead.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure and functions of the two complex tissues, xylem and phloem, naming their elements and saying which are living.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Xylem** conducts **water and minerals** from roots to leaves and gives mechanical support. Its elements are **tracheids** and **vessels** (dead, lignified, water-conducting), **xylem fibres** (dead, supporting) and **xylem parenchyma** (the only living element, storing food). The first-formed xylem is protoxylem and the later is metaxylem.

**Phloem** conducts **food** from the leaves to other parts. Its elements are **sieve tube elements** (long tubes with sieve plates, living but without a nucleus), **companion cells** (nucleated, helping the sieve tubes), **phloem parenchyma** (absent in most monocots) and **phloem fibres** (dead, sclerenchymatous).

questions.solution_md: Xylem and phloem elements, functions, living or dead.

marking_scheme.step: Xylem function and protoxylem or metaxylem

questions.stem_md: Describe the three tissue systems of a flowering plant with the tissues that make up each, and distinguish the types of vascular bundle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Epidermal system:** the epidermis, with a cuticle on aerial parts, stomata guarded by two guard cells (bean-shaped in dicots, dumbbell-shaped in grasses), root hairs and trichomes.

**Ground tissue system:** everything except the epidermis and vascular bundles: cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in stems and roots, and mesophyll in leaves.

**Vascular system:** xylem and phloem, with cambium in dicot stems. **Radial** bundles in roots have xylem and phloem on different radii. **Conjoint** bundles in stems and leaves have them on the same radius; they are **open** with cambium between them (dicot stems) or **closed** without cambium (monocot stems).

questions.solution_md: Three tissue systems and bundle types.

questions.stem_md: A leafy herbaceous shoot is cut under water and kept in red ink for two hours. Thin sections then show red colour in a part of each vascular bundle, but not in the cortex or pith. Name the tissue that carried the ink, its elements and their nature, say where in a dicot stem bundle the colour will appear, and predict what would happen to food movement if the phloem were cut.

answer.model_answer_md: The **xylem** carried the ink, as it conducts **water and minerals**. Its conducting elements are **tracheids and vessels**, which are **dead** with lignified walls; the fibres give support and xylem parenchyma is living. In a dicot stem the bundle is **conjoint and open**, with xylem on the **inner side** of the cambium, nearest the pith, so the colour appears there, with the **protoxylem towards the pith**. If the **phloem** were cut, **food from the leaves** could not be **conducted** to the roots and other parts, so sugars would pile up above the cut and the roots would starve, although water would still rise through the xylem.

questions.solution_md: Xylem, elements, position in a dicot bundle, effect of cutting phloem.

marking_scheme.step: Inner side of the open bundle; endarch
Phloem cut: food not conducted; water still rises

questions.passage_md: A student prepares a thin transverse section of a celery petiole and a squash of a pear fruit. In the petiole she sees a ring of cells beneath the epidermis with thickened corners; some contain chloroplasts. In the pear squash she finds clusters of hard, rounded cells with very thick walls. She photographs one of these cells at 900 times magnification, and it measures 36 mm across on the print.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) sclereids

**(b)** 40 micrometres

**(c)** (i) The petiole cells are **collenchyma**: **living**, with walls thickened only at the **corners** by cellulose and pectin, so they stay flexible and support growing parts. The pear cells are **sclerenchyma**: **dead**, with **thick lignified** walls and almost no cavity, so they are rigid and cannot stretch.

**OR** (ii) The soft flesh is mostly **parenchyma**, with living, thin-walled cells. In plants, parenchyma carries out **photosynthesis** (when it has chloroplasts), **storage** of food and **secretion**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Rounded, thick-walled, dead cells in the pulp of pear are sclereids — option (c).

**(b)** $\dfrac{36 \times 1000}{900} = 40$ micrometres.

**(c)** (i) Living flexible collenchyma versus dead rigid sclerenchyma.

(ii) Parenchyma; two functions.

questions.passage_md: A student takes epidermal peels from the upper and lower surfaces of a sunflower leaf and of a maize leaf. In the sunflower leaf, a field of 0.25 square millimetres shows 5 stomata on the upper peel and 20 on the lower peel. In the maize leaf, a field of 0.2 square millimetres shows 9 stomata on each peel.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) Sunflower guard cells are bean-shaped; maize guard cells are dumbbell-shaped.

**(b)** 45

**(c)** (i) Upper density is $\dfrac{5}{0.25} = 20$ and lower density is $\dfrac{20}{0.25} = 80$ per square millimetre, so the lower surface has **4 times** as many. This suggests a **dorsiventral** leaf, as in dicots, with most stomata on the lower side.

**(b)** $\dfrac{9}{0.2} = 45$ stomata per square millimetre.

**(c)** (i) Ratio 4; dorsiventral leaf.

(ii) Isobilateral; undifferentiated mesophyll.

questions.solution_md: Lateral roots arise from the pericycle, the layer just inside the endodermis — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A transverse section of a root shows eight patches of xylem alternating with eight of phloem, and a large pith. The root is
questions.solution_md: More than six xylem bundles (polyarch) and a large, well-developed pith indicate a monocot root — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A transverse section shows two to four patches of xylem alternating with phloem, a very small pith, and an endodermis with Casparian strips. The organ is
questions.solution_md: Few xylem patches (diarch to tetrarch), a small pith and an endodermis with Casparian strips are features of a dicot root — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a transverse section of a sunflower stem the vascular bundles lie in a ring. Which tissue lies between neighbouring bundles?
questions.solution_md: In a dicot stem the parenchyma between the bundles forms the medullary rays — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Below the epidermis of one stem section a student finds sclerenchyma; below the epidermis of another she finds collenchyma. The first stem is most probably

options.text_md: a dicot stem and the second a monocot stem
a monocot stem and the second a dicot stem
a dicot stem and the second also a dicot stem
a monocot stem and the second also a monocot stem

questions.solution_md: The hypodermis is sclerenchymatous in monocot stems and collenchymatous in dicot stems — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which feature will a student find in a maize stem but not in a sunflower stem?

options.text_md: Scattered bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous sheath
A ring of conjoint bundles with cambium in each
A collenchymatous hypodermis below the epidermis

questions.solution_md: Monocot stems have many scattered closed bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths; the other features belong to dicot stems — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The radial strips of parenchyma lying between the vascular bundles of a sunflower stem are called
questions.solution_md: The parenchyma between the bundles of dicot stems forms the medullary rays — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student wants to find where most of the chloroplasts lie in a transverse section of a dicot leaf. Which layer should she examine?

options.text_md: Palisade parenchyma, just below the upper epidermis
Spongy parenchyma, next to the lower epidermis
The upper epidermis, which is always full of chloroplasts
The bundle sheath around the vein

questions.solution_md: The palisade cells, tall and tightly packed below the upper epidermis, carry most of the chloroplasts — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A leaf peel shows about the same number of stomata on both surfaces, and the mesophyll is not divided into palisade and spongy parts. The leaf is
questions.solution_md: Stomata on both surfaces and undifferentiated mesophyll mark an isobilateral leaf, typical of monocots such as grasses — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Each vascular bundle in the veins of a leaf is surrounded by a layer of thick-walled cells called the
questions.solution_md: The vascular bundles of leaves are surrounded by a bundle sheath of thick-walled cells — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the lettered section of a dicot leaf, which letter marks the tall, closely packed cells just below the upper epidermis?
questions.solution_md: The palisade parenchyma, part A, forms tall, tightly packed cells below the upper epidermis — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The vascular bundles of a dicot stem are described as open.

**Reason (R):** A strip of cambium lies between the xylem and the phloem of each bundle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the presence of cambium between xylem and phloem is exactly what makes a conjoint bundle open — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a dicot leaf the palisade parenchyma lies just below the upper epidermis.

**Reason (R):** Palisade parenchyma has large air spaces between its cells.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: palisade cells are tightly packed; the large air spaces are in the spongy parenchyma — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Grass leaves roll inward when water is scarce.

**Reason (R):** Bulliform cells are small, thick-walled and lignified cells of the lower epidermis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells of the upper epidermis that lose turgor and let the leaf roll — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The pith of a monocot root is small and inconspicuous.

**Reason (R):** A monocot root has more than six patches of xylem, that is, it is polyarch.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: a monocot root has a large, well-developed pith. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The pith of a dicot root is large and well developed.
questions.solution_md: False. A dicot root has a small pith or none; a large pith is characteristic of the monocot root.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The vascular bundles of a monocot stem have no cambium.
questions.solution_md: True. They are conjoint and closed, surrounded by a sclerenchymatous sheath.

questions.stem_md: The Casparian strips in the endodermis of a root are bands of ______ in the cell walls.
questions.solution_md: Suberin.

questions.stem_md: Large, empty, colourless cells in the upper epidermis of a grass leaf, which help the leaf to roll, are called ______ cells.
questions.solution_md: Bulliform.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature (column I) with the organ in which it is found (column II).

options.text_md: Starch sheath as the innermost cortical layer

questions.solution_md: The starch sheath is the endodermis of the dicot stem; the water cavity occurs in monocot stem bundles; Casparian strips belong to the root; bulliform cells belong to the grass leaf.

questions.stem_md: A student counts 24 vascular bundles in a field of 4 square millimetres of a maize stem section. Assuming an even spread, how many bundles are in a section of 15 square millimetres?
questions.solution_md: Density: $\dfrac{24}{4} = 6$ per square millimetre; section: $6 \times 15 = 90$ bundles.

questions.stem_md: In a section of a dicot leaf the upper epidermis is 20 micrometres thick, the palisade layer 70, the spongy layer 90 and the lower epidermis 20. What is the thickness of the mesophyll, in micrometres?
questions.solution_md: Mesophyll = palisade + spongy $= 70 + 90 = 160$ micrometres.

questions.stem_md: A monocot root has 8 xylem arms alternating with an equal number of phloem patches. How many patches of vascular tissue (xylem and phloem together) are there in all?
questions.solution_md: Eight xylem patches and eight phloem patches: $2 \times 8 = 16$.

questions.stem_md: A student identifies 80 cells in a field of a stem section: 20 collenchyma, 44 parenchyma and 16 sclerenchyma. What percentage of the cells are collenchyma?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{20}{80} \times 100 = 25$ percent.

questions.stem_md: Describe the endodermis of a root and explain the role of the Casparian strips.

answer.model_answer_md: The **endodermis** is a single layer of **barrel-shaped** cells forming the innermost layer of the cortex. Its walls carry **Casparian strips**, bands of **suberin**, so water and minerals must pass through the **cytoplasm** of its cells, which lets the plant control what reaches the xylem.

questions.solution_md: Endodermis; Casparian strips make water pass through cells.

marking_scheme.step: Casparian strips of suberin; water must enter the cells

questions.stem_md: List four anatomical features of a monocot stem as seen in transverse section.

answer.model_answer_md: A **monocot stem** has a **sclerenchymatous hypodermis** and a large **undifferentiated ground tissue**. Its **vascular bundles are scattered**, each **conjoint and closed** with a **sclerenchymatous sheath**. **Phloem parenchyma is absent**, and a **water-containing cavity** is present in the bundle.

questions.solution_md: Four features of the monocot stem.

marking_scheme.step: Bundles scattered, closed, sheath; no phloem parenchyma

questions.stem_md: A student cuts a transverse section of a mustard leaf. Name the two kinds of mesophyll she will see and state one difference between them.

answer.model_answer_md: The mesophyll has **palisade parenchyma** and **spongy parenchyma**. The palisade cells are **elongated, tightly packed** and lie below the **upper** epidermis with many chloroplasts, whereas the spongy cells are **oval or round, loosely arranged** with **large air spaces**, towards the lower epidermis.

questions.solution_md: Palisade versus spongy.

questions.stem_md: In a dry spell a farmer notices that the leaves of his wheat plants curl inward. Which cells are involved, and how does the curling help the plant?

answer.model_answer_md: **Bulliform cells**, large, empty, colourless cells on the **upper epidermis**, lose water and **turgor**, so the leaf **rolls inward**. This exposes less surface to the air and so **minimises water loss** by transpiration.

questions.solution_md: Bulliform cells; rolling reduces water loss.

marking_scheme.step: Bulliform cells lose turgor; leaf rolls

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a dicot root from a monocot root on three anatomical points.

answer.model_answer_md: A **dicot root** has **two to four** xylem patches (diarch to tetrarch) and a **small pith**. A **monocot root** has **more than six** xylem bundles, that is **polyarch**, and a **large, well-developed pith**. In both, the xylem is **exarch**, the bundles are **radial**, and there is an endodermis with Casparian strips.

questions.solution_md: Number of xylem bundles; pith; shared features.

questions.stem_md: Describe the layers seen, from outside to inside, in a transverse section of a dicot stem up to the vascular bundles.

answer.model_answer_md: The outermost layer is the **epidermis** with a cuticle, a few stomata and multicellular trichomes. Below it is the **hypodermis** of a few layers of **collenchyma**. The **cortex** has several layers of parenchyma with intercellular spaces, and its innermost layer is the **endodermis** or **starch sheath**. Inside it lies the **pericycle**, often as **sclerenchyma** caps over the vascular bundles.

questions.solution_md: Epidermis, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a dorsiventral leaf from an isobilateral leaf on three points, naming the plant group in which each is usually found.

answer.model_answer_md: A **dorsiventral** leaf, usually of **dicots**, has **more stomata on the lower** epidermis and mesophyll divided into **palisade and spongy** parenchyma. An **isobilateral** leaf, usually of **monocots**, has **stomata on both** surfaces in about equal numbers and **undifferentiated** mesophyll, and its upper epidermis has **bulliform cells**.

questions.solution_md: Stomata, mesophyll, bulliform cells; plant groups.

questions.stem_md: Describe the anatomy of a dicot root as seen in transverse section, and state how a monocot root differs.

answer.model_answer_md:
From outside: the **epidermis** bears unicellular **root hairs**. The **cortex** has several layers of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces. The **endodermis** is a single layer of barrel-shaped cells with **Casparian strips** of suberin. The **pericycle**, a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma, gives rise to **lateral roots**. There are **two to four** patches of **exarch xylem** alternating with phloem, the **radial** arrangement, with **conjunctive tissue** between them, and a **small pith**.

A **monocot root** has the same plan, but **more than six** xylem bundles (polyarch) and a **large, well-developed pith**.

questions.solution_md: Layers of the dicot root; monocot differences.

marking_scheme.step: Radial exarch xylem and phloem, conjunctive tissue, pith

questions.stem_md: Compare the transverse sections of a dicot stem and a monocot stem on the hypodermis, the ground tissue, the vascular bundles and the phloem.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Hypodermis:** collenchymatous in the dicot stem; sclerenchymatous in the monocot stem.

**Ground tissue:** in the dicot stem it is differentiated into cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, medullary rays and a large pith. In the monocot stem it is a large, undifferentiated mass of parenchyma.

**Vascular bundles:** in the dicot stem they are few and arranged in a **ring**, conjoint, **open** (with cambium) and endarch. In the monocot stem they are **many and scattered**, conjoint and **closed**, each with a sclerenchymatous sheath, smaller and more numerous near the periphery.

**Phloem:** phloem parenchyma is present in the dicot stem and absent in the monocot stem; the monocot bundle has a water-containing cavity.

questions.solution_md: Four points of comparison.

questions.stem_md: Describe the anatomy of a dicot leaf as seen in transverse section, and state how an isobilateral leaf differs.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **upper and lower epidermis** are covered by a cuticle; the lower epidermis has **more stomata**, each with two bean-shaped guard cells. The **mesophyll**, between the epidermises, has **palisade parenchyma**, elongated, tightly packed cells below the upper epidermis rich in chloroplasts, and **spongy parenchyma**, loosely arranged cells with **large air spaces** towards the lower side. **Vascular bundles** in the veins are surrounded by a **bundle sheath**, with xylem towards the upper side and phloem towards the lower.

An **isobilateral** leaf has **stomata on both** surfaces, **undifferentiated** mesophyll and **bulliform cells** in the upper epidermis.

questions.solution_md: Layers of a dicot leaf; isobilateral leaf.

questions.stem_md: A student wrote these notes on three plant samples. Stem sample: “vascular bundles in a ring with cambium, so the bundles are closed.” Leaf sample: “palisade and spongy parenchyma are present, so it is an isobilateral leaf.” Root sample: “xylem lies towards the pith, so it is exarch.” Evaluate each statement, correct the errors, and say what the notes should have concluded in each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Stem.** Bundles in a ring with cambium are **open**, not closed; a closed bundle lacks cambium. The sample is probably a **dicot stem**. **Leaf.** Palisade and spongy parenchyma mean a **dorsiventral** leaf, not isobilateral; an isobilateral leaf has undifferentiated mesophyll. It is probably a dicot leaf. **Root.** Xylem with the protoxylem towards the **pith** is **endarch**, the stem pattern; exarch means protoxylem towards the periphery, as in roots. So the notes confuse the terms.

**Judgement.** All three statements are wrong: each conclusion contradicts the observation that was recorded.

questions.solution_md: Evaluates three statements; corrects each.

questions.passage_md: A student cuts a thin transverse section of a young root and examines it. She sees an epidermis bearing root hairs, a wide cortex, and a ring of cells inside it. Within this ring there are eight patches of xylem, each with its smallest vessels towards the outside, alternating with eight patches of phloem. At the centre is a large region of parenchyma.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) A monocot root, because the xylem is polyarch and the pith is large

**(b)** 16

**(c)** (i) The arrangement is **exarch**, the pattern of roots. The smallest vessels, towards the periphery, are the **protoxylem**, the first-formed xylem, while the larger vessels towards the centre are the **metaxylem**, formed later.

**OR** (ii) The central region is the **pith**, made of **parenchyma**. In this monocot root it is **large and well developed**, whereas in a **dicot root** the pith is **small** or may be absent.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** More than six xylem bundles and a large pith are typical of a monocot root — option (b).

**(b)** $8 + 8 = 16$ patches.

**(c)** (i) Exarch; protoxylem outside.

(ii) Large pith versus small pith.

questions.passage_md: A student cuts a transverse section of a stem and sees many vascular bundles scattered through a large mass of parenchyma. Each bundle is surrounded by a ring of thick-walled cells, and contains xylem and phloem but no cambium. In a field of 4 square millimetres she counts 24 bundles. The bundles are smaller and closer together near the outer edge.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Conjoint and closed

**(b)** 6

**(c)** (i) This is a **monocot stem**. Further confirmation comes from the **sclerenchymatous hypodermis**, the **undifferentiated ground tissue**, the **absence of phloem parenchyma** and a **water-containing cavity** in the bundles.

**OR** (ii) The bundles are **not evenly spread**: they are **smaller and more crowded near the periphery** and fewer, larger ones lie near the centre. A count from one field therefore does not represent the whole section, so scaling it up gives only an **estimate**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Xylem and phloem on the same radius with no cambium make a conjoint, closed bundle, typical of a monocot stem — option (a).

**(b)** $\dfrac{24}{4} = 6$ bundles per square millimetre.

**(c)** (i) Monocot stem and two more features.

(ii) Uneven distribution of bundles.
